pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: A teammate says a container is a lightweight virtual machine. What do you tell them? Name the two kernel mechanisms and what each one controls.
expected_points: a container is an ordinary host process, not a guest machine
namespaces restrict what it can see: PID tree, mount/filesystem root, network interfaces and ports, hostname, user IDs
cgroups restrict what it can use: CPU, memory, I/O limits
a VM boots a second kernel on emulated hardware; a container shares the host kernel, so it starts in milliseconds
consequences: Linux images need a Linux kernel (Docker runs a hidden Linux VM on macOS/Windows), and isolation is thinner than a VM's

questions.prompt: What is the difference between an image and a container? Where do files your program writes at run time actually go?
expected_points: image is a read-only stack of layers plus metadata; it is inert
container is that image plus a thin writable layer plus a running process
one image can back many containers, each with its own writable layer
run-time writes land in the writable layer, never in the image
docker rm deletes the writable layer, so that data is gone; volumes exist for data you keep

questions.prompt: You built your image, then changed one line in main.go and rebuilt. Which instructions were cached and which re-ran — and why does copying go.mod before the source matter?
expected_points: cache key is parent layer plus the instruction, plus file contents for COPY/ADD
FROM, WORKDIR, COPY go.mod and go mod download hit the cache since nothing they depend on changed
COPY . . misses because the copied files changed, and the first miss invalidates every instruction after it
copying the whole tree first would drag go mod download into the miss and re-download dependencies on every edit

questions.prompt: Why is `latest` not a version, and what does pinning by digest buy you that a tag cannot?
expected_points: latest is just the default tag name, not a claim about recency
tags are mutable pointers the publisher can move at any time
concrete example of harm: identical source builds differently on two days, and the old image cannot be reproduced or bisected
a digest is the SHA-256 of the image content, an immutable identity
cost of digests: you own updating them, usually via an automated pull request

questions.prompt: Walk me through building your image and getting a request answered from your host — then stopping and removing it. Which command does what, and what does -p 8080:8080 actually do?
expected_points: docker build -t name:tag . where . is the build context sent to the daemon
docker run -d -p host:container publishes a port from the container's own network namespace onto the host
docker ps / docker ps -a to see running and stopped containers; docker logs reads stdout and stderr
docker exec runs an extra process inside the existing container, for debugging
docker stop sends SIGTERM then SIGKILL; docker rm deletes the container and its writable layer
EXPOSE is documentation and does not publish anything

questions.prompt: How does an image get from your laptop to another machine? Read me the parts of `ghcr.io/ada/clockwork:1.4.0`.
expected_points: registry host / repository / tag, with Docker Hub assumed when the registry is omitted
docker login, docker tag to the target repository, docker push; docker pull (or an implicit pull on run) on the other side
pushing is normally CI's job rather than a laptop's
layers are shared and content-addressed, so a shared base is transferred once

questions.prompt: A Dockerfile does `COPY secrets.env .` and later `RUN rm secrets.env`. Is the secret in the published image?
expected_points: yes — the delete only writes a whiteout marker in a later layer
the bytes remain in the earlier layer and anyone who pulls the image can extract them
the fix is to keep it out of the build context entirely (.dockerignore), not to delete it afterwards

questions.prompt: Why does `CMD ["/bin/app"]` behave differently from `CMD /bin/app` when someone runs `docker stop`?
expected_points: shell form runs /bin/sh -c, so the shell is PID 1 and your binary is its child
a plain sh does not forward signals, so SIGTERM never reaches your program
after the grace period everything is SIGKILLed mid-flight; exec form makes your binary PID 1 and it receives the signal directly
